newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says children still at risk from lead.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says children still at risk from lead.

text.p: The amount of lead in Americans' blood has declined over the past two decades, but nearly a million children still have elevated blood lead levels, federal health officials said Thursday.

The U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said a national survey found declines in blood lead levels in every segment of the American population. Average blood levels have dropped more than 80 percent since the late 1970s.

However, the agency said about 930,000 children aged one to five years had blood levels that have been associated with adverse health effects. "There are still children who we are missing," CDC research statistician Debra Brodey said.
Young children absorb lead more readily than adults. Lead poses a particular risk to their developing nervous systems.

The number of children with elevated blood levels, defined as 10 micrograms per deciliter, has fallen 51 percent since the late 1970s. Most of the chidren with excessive lead levels live with low-income families or in houses built before 1946, when lead-based paints may have been used, the CDC said.

"We have achieved average blood lead levels which would have been considered impossible just a few decades ago," Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said. "But a significant number of children are still at risk for high lead exposure."
The CDC is proposing new guidelines for screening young children that target children who live in older homes or who are from low-income families.

"We want to increase screening and follow-up care for those children who are at risk," CDC director Dr. David Satcher said. "The best way to do this is through state and local public health decision-makers. The proposed guidelines will help them bring about effective screening and follow-up care for children."
The agency said the declines in blood lead levels have occurred because of the removal of lead from gasoline, household paint, food and drink cans and plumbing systems.

The national survey conducted between 1991 and 1994 found that more than one-fifth of non-Hispanic black children living in older homes have elevated blood lead levels. The agency blamed deteriorating paint in older housing, dust and soil contaminated by paint and residues from past emissions of leaded gasoline, which was banned two decades ago.
